body:
## Problem

Defining a mapping to "repeat last motion", is not 100% perfect, because e.g. `type=mapping` and `type=ex` CmdAtoms may not clearly indicate that they are motions. It *is* possible to filter by `type==motion or (type==mapping and changed==false)`, but that doesn't capture complex mappings or interactive ":" cmdline invocations.

Example:

```lua
_G.my_motion = function() vim.api.nvim_win_set_cursor(0, { 2, 0 }) end
```

Example using "mini.bracketed" plugin: `]c` is mapped to `<Cmd>lua MiniBracketed.comment('forward')<CR>`. The emitted event is:

```lua
{
  cascade = false,
  changed = false,
  cmd = "<Cmd>",
  keys = "<Cmd>lua MiniBracketed.comment('forward')\n",
  lhs = "]c",
  text = "lua MiniBracketed.comment('forward')",
  type = "ex"
}
```

`type = "ex"` describes the RHS implementation, not the "semantic" user action.

Rejected workarounds:

- Filter by `type == "mapping" and changed == false`. Excludes text edits, but does not exclude other non-motion actions.
- Inspect the subatoms types (`CmdAtom.atoms`).
    - Not provided for the above example: a single-subatom composite is "unwrapped". `atoms` is
non-`nil` only for multi-command mappings.
    - ~~TBD: we could just not "unwrap"? that seems simpler...~~ Doesn't help, just adds an extra nesting level with no useful info.
- Only consider motions invoked from a mapping.
    - User also wants to repeat motions emited by interactive ":" cmdline commands/function calls.

## Expected behavior

### Ideas

- `setrepeat()` (placeholder name) allows plugins to announce hints about the "current user action": `type=motion`, `namespace='my.plugin'`
- leverage the "keymap namespace" / "plugin namespace" concepts: plugins define mappings via `vim.keymap.set{namespace=...}`, and `CmdAtom` events include a `CmdAtom.namespace` field .
    - #32261

### Requirements?

- Nvim emits, plugins annotate. Plugins should not fake `CmdAtom` events. `nvim_exec_autocmds('CmdAtom', …)` currently "works" but this may be the wrong direction...
- Keep true dot-repeat separate from customizable repeat. If plugins can annotate the "current user action", then there is no *reason* that plugins need to modify the "." redo buffer?

### Other todo

- `type = "ex"` → `excmd`.
- `type = "command"` is too vague; needs a better name.

comment_data.body:
I think this can be achieved with better classification by Nvim itself, except for e.g. async motion (`vim.schedule`). For that, we will need namespaces (`vim.keymap.set{namespace=...}`).

I don't really see the cmdline ":" case as important, but that could also be solved by a namespace somehow.

The main motivation behind this is that I'd want users to be able to make a "repeat last motion" mapping that 1) works with both built-in and custom motions; and 2) doesn't require tedious book-keeping on the user side:

- By "repeat last motion" mapping I mostly mean the current content of `:h motion-repeat` which creates a `,` mapping by observing `CmdAtom` event for `type='motion'` events and repeating them with `nvim_feedkeys`.

- By 1 I mostly mean plugins that implement custom motions (like "move to next/previous/first/last comment/hunk/conflict/etc").

- By 2 I mostly mean that (ideally) users should not need to manually keep track of which motions they'd want to be repeat-able, while (ideally) it should be possible to opt-out for certain motions. Otherwise it adds a load on both plugins (commit to and document a special namespace) and user (not only install a plugin but also not forget to add its motions to a special mapping).

---

To make things more grounded, here is the toy example of custom motions that differ in how they are implemented and how they are exposed to the user (all repro is on the latest master, 31de0d69fc, after #41386):

1. An exported function that uses API calls; mapped with `<Cmd>...<CR>` RHS:

    <details><summary>Code and `CmdAtom` data</summary>

    Code:

    ```lua
    _G.motion_2 = function()
      local cur = vim.api.nvim_win_get_cursor(0)
      vim.api.nvim_win_set_cursor(0, { cur[1] + 2, cur[2] })
    end
    vim.keymap.set('n', ']2', '<Cmd>lua _G.motion_2()<CR>')
    ```

    Typing `]2` currently triggers a single `CmdAtom` event with the following `data`:

    ```lua
    {
      cascade = false,
      changed = false,
      cmd = "<Cmd>",
      keys = "<80><fd>hlua _G.motion_2()\n",
      lhs = "]2",
      text = "lua _G.motion_2()",
      type = "ex"
    }
    ```

    </details>

2. A private function that uses `normal!` command of what is recognized as a motion; mapped with callback RHS:

    <details><summary>Code and `CmdAtom` data</summary>

    Code:

    ```lua
    local motion_3 = function() vim.cmd('normal! 2j') end
    vim.keymap.set('n', ']3', motion_3)
    ```

    Typing `]3` currently triggers a single `CmdAtom` event with the following `data`:

    ```lua
    {
      cascade = false,
      changed = false,
      keys = "",
      lhs = "]3",
      type = "mapping"
    }
    ```

    </details>

3. A user command that is implemented as different `normal!` commands:

    <details><summary>Code and `CmdAtom` data</summary>

    Code:

    ```lua
    local motion_4 = function()
      vim.cmd('normal! 2j')
      vim.cmd('normal! 2j')
    end
    vim.api.nvim_create_user_command('Motion4', motion_4, {})
    ```

    Typing `:Motion4`-`<CR>` currently triggers a single `CmdAtom` event with the following `data`:

    ```lua
    {
      cascade = false,
      changed = false,
      cmd = ":",
      keys = ":Motion4\n",
      lhs = ":Motion4\n",
      text = "Motion4",
      type = "ex"
    }
    ```

    </details>

4. A global Lua function that uses `feedkeys`:

    <details><summary>Code and `CmdAtom` data</summary>

    Code:

    ```lua
    _G.motion_5 = function() vim.fn.feedkeys('5j', 'n') end
    ```

    Typing `:lua _G.motion_5()`-`<CR>` currently triggers a single `CmdAtom` event with the following `data`:

    ```lua
    {
      cascade = false,
      changed = false,
      cmd = ":",
      keys = ":lua _G.motion_5()\n",
      lhs = ":lua _G.motion_5()\n",
      text = "lua _G.motion_5()",
      type = "ex"
    }
    ```

    </details>

I would argue that each of these examples represent a valid implementation *and* usage of a custom motion. And that (ideally) there should exist a way to make them be treated by the user like their built-in counterparts (`2j`, `3j`, `4j`, `5j`). However:

- Neither of them actually convey the information that the performed action/atom is a motion.

- The mapping with the callback RHS doesn't have enough information to be repeated.

---

What I think is the most promising direction here is to expose for users/plugins a way to say "Hey, I just performed a motion/jump/etc. Here is all the data you need to know about it." which they will do along with doing the action. And not only for repeating purposes (i.e. `setrepeat` route ideally is not enough), but also for all sorts of possible hooks (logging, auto-adjust, etc.).

First thing that comes to mind is autocommand approach. Adding something like `vim.api.nvim_exec_autocmds('CmdAtom', { pattern = 'motion', data = { type = 'motion', keys = '<80><fd>hlua _G.motion_2()\n' } }) ` after performing a motion seems to work. If mixing `CmdAtom` with custom motions doesn't sound good, then maybe a new `CmdAtomUser` event or a flag/enum in event data indicating source?

> What I think is the most promising direction here is to expose for users/plugins a way to say "Hey, I just performed a motion/jump/etc. Here is all the data you need to know about it."

That is not a good *general* approach, because it requires every plugin to do that, which is lame (besides being unrealistic and clumsy). The editor should figure it out *automatically*, that's the entire purpose of atoms. 

Yes, we'll need an *escape hatch* for edge cases I guess, but this should not be the central mechanism.

> it adds a load on both plugins (commit to and document a special namespace) and user (not only install a plugin but also not forget to add its motions to a special mapping).

Namespaces can be declared as part of the mapping/`:command` declaration. How is that more of a "load" than having to change the implementation itself?

Users generally won't need to care unless they are very picky about which atoms they want to act upon (and then namespaces are totally reasonable).

> > it adds a load on both plugins (commit to and document a special namespace) and user (not only install a plugin but also not forget to add its motions to a special mapping).
> 
> Namespaces can be declared as part of the mapping/`:command` declaration. How is that more of a "load" than having to change the implementation itself?

The namespaced keymaps approach:

- Plugin side:
    - Add `vim.keymap.set('n', ']2', rhs, { namespace = vim.api.nvim_create_namespace('myplugin.motion') })`.
    - Add documentation "Namespace `myplugin.motion` represents mappings for motions".
- User side:
    - Make `CmdAtom` event that tracks `motion` type plus `'myplugin.motion'` namespace (plus `'otherplugin.motion'`, plus `'anotherplugin.motion'`, plus etc.).
- Additional notes:
    - Works only in mappings.
    - Users have to add those or custom namespaces if they want to make keymaps themselves.
    - Tracking namespaces requires an extra layer of `vim.api.nvim_get_namespaces()['myplugin.motion']`. Which is not ideal.

The "plugin advertises motion `CmdAtom`" approach:

- Plugin side:
    - Add `<advertise motion CmdAtom>` snippet after performing a motion. Would contain `ev.data.keys` that is enough to repeat the motion.
- User side:
    - Make `CmdAtom` event that tracks `motion` type.
- Additional notes:
    - Works in mappings, commands, interactive calls.

> Users generally won't need to care unless they are very picky about which atoms they want to act upon (and then namespaces are totally reasonable).

With how things currently are, either users will have to care to add certain namespaces to the "repeat last motion" mapping snippet or plugins will have to care to advertise motion action.

---

In any way, I think the above motion implementations are enough to serve as a yard stick of how easy/hard/impossible it is to make "repeat last motion" work with custom motions. Ideally, it would require from the user to only track the `au CmdAtom motion ...` for the last motion. How much more complex it would be with custom motions is an open question/target.

> Works only in mappings.

Also works for commands (`nvim_create_user_command` can take a namespace). Which covers most "user actions"...

> Users have to add those or custom namespaces if they want to make keymaps themselves.

If they are very particular about repeating only specific atoms which aren't already properly classified (which still can be improved, and there is another PR incoming) ... then yes.

https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/41414 closes this.

- It greatly improves `CmdAtom.lhs`, so it consistently means "the *user intention*", i.e. it includes chars collected by `getchar()` during a mapping. That is a big improvement to the semantics of CmdAtom.
- It provides a `CmdAtom.moved` flag which users can check to decide whether an atom is a "motion".
    - Of course, that will have "false negatives" if the cursor didn't actually move (e.g. `G` at EOB). I have further work planned to improve the `type=motion` classification, but it won't be perfect.

I can't stop plugins from publishing `CmdAtom` (actually I can, by removing `ev.data.type`), but I think it's an "XY solution" and we should try to focus on a holistic, "just works" solution. 

Try `CmdAtom.moved` for a few days, to see if it's good enough. Let's try to see the *actual size* of the problem, rather than insisting on this idea that users absolutely, perfectly must know whether every single thing is a "motion". Something that works 99% of the time is going to feel great, users aren't going to care about a false negative.

Allowing *namespace* annotations is a separate topic, I'll open a new issue focused on that.

> To make things more grounded, here is the toy example of custom motions that differ in how they are implemented and how they are exposed to the user

After https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/41414 ,

- Examples 1-3 are correctly detected by checking `moved and not changed and not operator`.
- Example 4 reports `moved=false` because `feedkeys('5j', 'n')` does not use the "t" flag (which is contrary to the idea of a "user action").
    - Workaround: Use the "t" or "x" flag. ("t" is recommended since `CmdAtom` represents "user input")
    - Workaround: use `vim.cmd('normal! 5j')` instead.
- All 4 examples replay correctly using the snippet at `:help cmdatom`.


<details>
<summary>And here is the CmdAtom events look like:</summary>

1. `<Cmd>` RHS mapping

```lua
{
  changed = false,
  cmd = "<Cmd>",
  keys = "<80><fd>hlua _G.motion_2()\n",
  lhs = "]2",
  moved = true,
  pos = { 1, 0 },
  text = "lua _G.motion_2()",
  type = "excmd",
  undoseq = 1,
}
```

2. Callback RHS

```lua
{
  changed = false,
  keys = "",
  lhs = "]3",
  moved = true,
  pos = { 1, 0 },
  remap = true,
  type = "mapping",
  undoseq = 1,
}
```

3. User command

```lua
{
  changed = false,
  cmd = ":",
  keys = ":Motion4\n",
  lhs = ":Motion4\n",
  moved = true,
  pos = { 1, 0 },
  text = "Motion4",
  type = "excmd",
  undoseq = 1,
}
```

4. `feedkeys` from `:lua`

```lua
{
  changed = false,
  cmd = ":",
  keys = ":lua _G.motion_5()\n",
  lhs = ":lua _G.motion_5()\n",
  moved = false,          -- << see above
  pos = { 1, 0 },
  text = "lua _G.motion_5()",
  type = "excmd",
  undoseq = 1,
}
```


</details>

> Of course, that will have "false negatives" if the cursor didn't actually move (e.g. `G` at EOB). I have further work planned to improve the `type=motion` classification, but it won't be perfect.
> ...
> Something that works 99% of the time is going to feel great, users aren't going to care about a false negative.
> ...
> Let's try to see the _actual size_ of the problem, rather than insisting on this idea that users absolutely, perfectly must know whether every single thing is a "motion".

Well, if the goal is "repeat last motion" I think it is reasonable to ask to be able to tell whether certain action is a motion or not. Detecting if the cursor has moved is indeed 90% solution, but my initial feeling that the rest 10% (attempted a motion but cursor didn't move and `vim.schedule()`ed motion`) *will* be rather annoying. Especially with custom motions which are not necessarily known in advance.

> Try `CmdAtom.moved` for a few days

I've tried it briefly and it seems to work without obvious issues with custom motions. The increased complexity of `,` mapping is a bit unfortunate, though.

> And here is the CmdAtom events look like:
> 
> `<Cmd>` RHS mapping

It is not quite right. It triggers two `CmdAtom` events: one `type='mapping'` and one `type='excmd'`. Not sure if that is intended and good/bad, but it is like this.

https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/41427 simplifies the `,` mapping a bit, and further improves how CmdAtom captures an end-to-end "user action", even for crazy stuff. It actually works much better than vim-repeat, now.

> [#41427](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/41427) simplifies the `,` mapping a bit, and further improves how CmdAtom captures an end-to-end "user action", even for crazy stuff. It actually works much better than vim-repeat, now.

My main hope is that it doesn't break all existing (and valid) dot-repeat approaches. Primarily an "expression mapping that constructs and returns `<Cmd>lua ...<CR>`".

All existing dot-repeat approaches are hacks. But `CmdAtom` can't "break" them anyway, because it's just an event. However, legacy dot-repeat approaches will be holding back the ecosystem, and should be disabled in Nvim 0.13.

> All existing dot-repeat approaches are hacks.

Hard disagree on the absolutism of the statement. Hijacking `.` mapping - yeah, sure. Creating mappings that work with built-in dot-repeat - maybe not straightforward at first, but not a hack at all.

> But `CmdAtom` can't "break" them anyway, because it's just an event. However, legacy dot-repeat approaches will be holding back the ecosystem, and should be disabled in Nvim 0.13.

My concern is about the documented "super `.` that works with any edit". Skimming through docs I have a feeling that it might break mappings that use `getcharstr()`, but we'll see.

Are you using vim-repeat or anything like that, or just a mapping that somehow checks state and returns a `<cmd>..<cr>` when it thinks the user wants to dot-repeat? Or something else? 



> "super `.` that works with any edit". Skimming through docs I have a feeling that it might break mappings that use `getcharstr()`

We'll need to make that work too (if it doesn't already; I really need concrete examples). No more hacks.

> "expression mapping that constructs and returns `<Cmd>lua ...<CR>`"

IIUC, I added a [test for this](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/compare/2b61afce3da25f63995296134ed169eacd5ca4fe..c922ab92c15af4256d88ac0e3d6581e95e9a42ac) (in https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/41427), it is working.

> Are you using vim-repeat or anything like that, or just a mapping that somehow checks state and returns a `<cmd>..<cr>` when it thinks the user wants to dot-repeat? Or something else?

No `vim-repeat`, nothing else, nothing "checks when user wants to dot-repeat". Just an expression mapping that returns a `<Cmd>lua ...<CR>`. The basic example:

```lua
_G.move_down = function(n) vim.cmd('normal! ' .. n .. 'j') end
local rhs = function() return string.format('<Cmd>lua _G.move_down(%d)<CR>', tonumber(vim.fn.getcharstr())) end
vim.keymap.set('o', '<Leader>jj', rhs, { expr = true })
```

Then doing something like `d` - `<Leader>jj` - `3` will delete three lines down. Pressing `.` any time later (if no other dot-repeatable action was done) will also delete `3` lines down.

This is the common approach I use for making dot-repeatable motions and textobjects. Has been working for at least five years now.

> We'll need to make that work too (if it doesn't already; I really need concrete examples). No more hacks.

I genuinely hope so. Otherwise supporting two ways to make dot-repeat will be difficult for plugins that want not only support Nightly.

> [#41427](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/41427) simplifies the `,` mapping a bit, and further improves how CmdAtom captures an end-to-end "user action", even for crazy stuff. It actually works much better than vim-repeat, now.

After that PR the documented `,` mapping in `:h motion-repeat` doesn't work with examples from this issue. In particular, no `CmdAtom pattern='motion'` event is triggered for any of the OP mappings/approaches. There are still `excmd` and `mapping` events with `data.moved = true`, but that doesn't fit into documented approach. So I'm not sure if that is a documentation or implementation issue.

Replacing the tracking bit with the following seems to make it work:

```lua
local last ---@type vim.event.cmdatom.data?
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('CmdAtom', {
  callback = function(ev)
    if ev.data.moved and not (ev.data.changed or ev.data.lhs == ',') then
      last = ev.data
    end
  end,
})
```

May need to adjust docs to deemphasize the `type=...` field. It is a best-effort classifier. 

Nvim could be smarter about classifying excmd/lua mappings, especially `<expr>` mappings, based on their resolved `keys`, e.g. if a excmd/lua mapping produces only "motion" keys then it could classify the composite atom as `type=motion`. I'm not sure that's going to satisfy all cases though.

> May need to adjust docs to deemphasize the `type=...` field. It is a best-effort classifier.
> 
> Nvim could be smarter about classifying excmd/lua mappings, especially `<expr>` mappings, based on their resolved `keys`, e.g. if a excmd/lua mapping produces only "motion" keys then it could classify the composite atom as `type=motion`. I'm not sure that's going to satisfy all cases though.

I think only relying on `ev.data.moved and not (ev.data.changed or ev.data.lhs == ',')` condition for all types is intuitive enough solution for classifying `CmdAtom` as motion.

title: CmdAtom: user can easily filter atoms by "motion" type

type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality
type.name: Enhancement
